title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=300 tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation. The study used a curated multi‑vendor (Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista) 300‑task intent manifest, a frozen validator encoding syntactic, interface‑assignment, basic reachability and destructive‑pattern checks, and the declared model snapshot gpt-5-mini. Under the preregistered paired design (shared initial candidate per task) every initial candidate passed the validator (baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300; n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0). The paired difference is 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% CI [0.00, 0.00]). Because no initial failures occurred, the guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked and no repair diagnostics were produced. We publish all raw outputs, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, the 300‑task manifest, and analysis artifacts (hash‑signed) to support reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, validator scope, and model family.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are proposed for converting operator intent into vendor CLI configurations to simplify NetOps workflows. Practical deployments often insert deterministic validators and bounded repair loops to reduce operational risk. We ask: does a bounded, deterministic G‑V‑R pipeline materially increase the fraction of validator‑passing configurations relative to direct generation? We preregistered a paired test that (a) generates one shared initial candidate per task, (b) scores baseline success if the initial candidate passes a deterministic validator, and (c) scores guarded success if the same initial candidate passes or, if it fails, a single automatic repair candidate passes. This manuscript reports the frozen preregistration, complete execution artifacts, and confirmatory analysis.
sections.related_work: We position this study amid LLM→NetOps and validation literature. Representative verified sources used for framing and nearest‑work comparisons include Nguyen et al. (2024) on intent‑based translation (intent→configuration), Chakraborty et al. (CNSM 2024) and Mondal et al. (2025) on LLM‑assisted configuration automation, and verification work such as Weitz et al. (2016) on SMT‑based policy verification. Recent benchmark efforts (NetLLMBench, 2024) motivated careful task design and validator definitions. These references were consulted and verified during the autonomous literature pass; we cite a compact, relevant subset in References.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e (frozen before execution). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Design: paired binary outcomes on n=300 curated tasks. For each task we produced one initial candidate (shared across arms). Baseline = validator(initial). Guarded = validator(initial) OR validator(repair) where at most one automatic repair call is allowed. The preregistered artifacts are published and hash‑signed (task manifest: execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3; model configuration: execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa; transformation manifest: execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256 = ef4f9a7e6e5e67398eca449221f29490ff0a107c38e2fd07cf833f9c35e4971a). Validator: scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). The validator artifact, scoring traces and example validator outputs are embedded under execution/scoring/*.json (representative examples cited below). Model and prompts: declared snapshot gpt-5-mini; shared initial generation only (one model call per task). Execution accounting and hashes are in the execution manifest. Analysis plan: two‑sided exact McNemar test for the primary estimand and paired bootstrap percentile CI (10k resamples, seed=1729). All analysis code and outputs were archived.

Primary outcome: every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator. Baseline_success_count = 300/300 (rate = 1.00); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (rate = 1.00). Paired contingency table: n11=300, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0). Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729; analysis log archived). Repair usage: the guarded policy invoked zero repair calls because the initial pass rate was 100%; hence the pre‑specified single‑repair policy was not exercised and repair‑success diagnostics are vacuous.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and implications. The run produced a ceiling outcome: the declared model snapshot and prompt regime generated initial candidates that satisfied the deterministic validator for every curated task; consequently the bounded guarded policy could not change outcomes. Statistically, when there are zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0) the paired test provides no evidence of a nonzero effect; the observed p=1.00 and collapsed CI reflect this degenerate but data‑valid result. Operationally, the absence of measurable guarded benefit in this run does not imply G‑V‑R is always unnecessary: measurable benefit requires (a) a nonzero initial failure rate under the chosen generator/prompt/model, (b) a validator whose coverage includes the failure modes the generator exhibits, or (c) a more aggressive repair policy. Design choice note (required revision addressed): the preregistered paired design used a shared initial candidate per task (one model call per task shared across baseline and guarded). That choice isolates the marginal effect of repair on a fixed initial sample; it also means that if the single initial draw passes the validator for every task (as observed), the guarded arm cannot improve outcomes under the predeclared single‑repair budget. For follow‑ups we recommend varying (i) task hardness (adversarial/OOD tasks), (ii) validator scope (augment deterministic checks with simulation/emulation or deeper routing semantics), (iii) model family and snapshot, and (iv) generation design (independent repeated draws per condition) to measure generator variability and repair utility. Reproducibility: all raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, task manifest, and analysis artifacts are published and hash‑signed; representative scoring examples are embedded below (paths and canonical SHA‑256 values are included).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired confirmatory evaluation of a bounded G‑V‑R policy on a 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest. Under the declared model snapshot and validator, every initial candidate passed the deterministic validator; therefore the guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked and no marginal improvement was observed (paired difference = 0.00; p = 1.00; 95% CI [0.00, 0.00]). The operational value of G‑V‑R depends on generator error rate, validator coverage and task hardness. All run artifacts (task manifest, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, analysis artifacts) are published and hash‑signed to enable reproducible follow‑ups that change one or more of the above factors.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface invariants, workflow ordering, destructive‑pattern detection) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; the chosen prompt/model snapshot produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting the ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered single‑repair policy.
Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this prevents measuring generator variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not tested.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary flagged zero pairs for exclusion but residual uncertainty remains.
